## Evaluation of $\displaystyle I = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\cos x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx$ via the Residue Theorem

### Step 1. Choose the auxiliary complex function

Consider
$$
f(z)=\frac{z\,e^{iz}}{1+z^{2}}.
$$
On the real axis, $z=x$, so
$$
f(x)=\frac{x\,e^{ix}}{1+x^{2}}=\frac{x\cos x}{1+x^{2}}+i\,\frac{x\sin x}{1+x^{2}}.
$$
Hence
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=\underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\cos x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx}_{I}+i\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\sin x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx.
$$
So $I=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx\right)$.

### Step 2. Set up the contour

Let $C_{R}$ be the closed contour consisting of the segment $[-R,R]$ on the real axis together with the upper semicircle $\Gamma_{R}=\{Re^{i\theta}:0\le\theta\le\pi\}$, traversed counterclockwise. For $R>1$ the contour encloses the pole of $f$ at $z=i$ (the pole at $z=-i$ lies in the lower half-plane).

### Step 3. Locate poles and compute the residue

The denominator factors as $1+z^{2}=(z-i)(z+i)$, giving simple poles at $z=\pm i$. Only $z=i$ lies inside $C_{R}$.

$$
\operatorname{Res}_{z=i}f(z)=\lim_{z\to i}(z-i)\frac{z\,e^{iz}}{(z-i)(z+i)}=\frac{z\,e^{iz}}{z+i}\bigg|_{z=i}=\frac{i\,e^{i\cdot i}}{2i}=\frac{e^{-1}}{2}=\frac{1}{2e}.
$$

### Step 4. Apply the residue theorem

$$
\oint_{C_{R}}f(z)\,dz=2\pi i\cdot\operatorname{Res}_{z=i}f(z)=2\pi i\cdot\frac{1}{2e}=\frac{\pi i}{e}.
$$

### Step 5. Show the arc integral vanishes

On $\Gamma_{R}$, write $z=Re^{i\theta}$. Since $\frac{z}{1+z^{2}}\to 0$ as $|z|\to\infty$ (it is $O(1/R)$), and $e^{iz}=e^{iR\cos\theta-R\sin\theta}$ decays exponentially in the upper half-plane ($\sin\theta\ge 0$), **Jordan's lemma** gives
$$
\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{\Gamma_{R}}\frac{z\,e^{iz}}{1+z^{2}}\,dz=0.
$$

### Step 6. Take the limit and extract the real part

Letting $R\to\infty$,
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\,e^{ix}}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{\pi i}{e}.
$$
Taking real parts of both sides:
$$
I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\cos x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{\pi i}{e}\right)=0.
$$
(The imaginary part simultaneously yields $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\sin x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{e}$.)

### Consistency check

The integrand $\frac{x\cos x}{1+x^{2}}$ is an **odd** function of $x$ (odd × even ÷ even = odd). Therefore the integral over the symmetric interval $(-\infty,\infty)$ must vanish, confirming $I=0$.
